name: two-species-community
title: Two-species cross-feeding community
question: When a glucose specialist and an acetate specialist share a single glucose/acetate pool with no spatial separation, does CRM-constrained dynamic FBA reproduce niche differentiation by cross-feeding — i.e. does the glucose specialist's acetate overflow sustain distinct, temporally offset growth of the acetate specialist — rather than simple competitive exclusion?
hypothesis: The glucose specialist (high glucose Vmax, tight O2 cap that forces acetate overflow) blooms first and draws glucose to zero while secreting acetate into the shared pool; the acetate specialist (high acetate Vmax, low glucose affinity) then does the majority of its growth on that byproduct, producing two temporally offset growth phases — the signature of cross-feeding-driven niche partitioning.
objective: Simulate the two-species crm_fba_community composite on the E. coli core GSM and measure per-species biomass and the shared glucose/acetate pools to determine whether the acetate specialist's growth is sustained by the glucose specialist's acetate overflow (niche differentiation) rather than by direct competition for glucose.
description:
A single glucose/acetate pool is shared by two E. coli core genome-scale models with no spatial separation. Each species is its own CRMProcess -> FBAStep pair: a Monod consumer-resource layer sets per-resource uptake targets from the current pool, and dynamic FBA turns those targets into exchange bounds, solves for growth, and writes realized substrate deltas back to the shared pool. Because both FBA steps read and write the same substrates store, one species' overflow becomes the other's feedstock.

The glucose specialist has high glucose Vmax, low acetate Vmax, and a tight oxygen cap (EX_o2_e lower = -6). Under that O2 limitation the LP cannot fully oxidize its glucose influx and secretes acetate as overflow — a Crabtree-like phenotype. The acetate specialist has low glucose affinity and high acetate Vmax, so it grows poorly on glucose but well on the acetate the first species leaks. The prediction is niche partitioning: an early glucose-driven bloom of the first species that builds an acetate pool, followed by a later acetate-driven bloom of the second.

The study runs the composite from a 15 mM glucose / 0 mM acetate pool with a 4:1 initial biomass split favouring the glucose specialist, records per-species biomass and the two shared pools, and checks three behaviours: glucose is drawn to zero, the acetate pool shows a transient overflow peak, and the acetate specialist does the majority of its growth after that peak.
claim: The glucose specialist's acetate overflow sustains a distinct acetate specialist: 93% of the acetate specialist's biomass gain occurs after the acetate pool peaks, and glucose is exhausted exactly at the peak (t=8.3) — niche differentiation by cross-feeding, not competitive exclusion.

assumptions.text: Monod kinetics adequately describe per-resource uptake targets for each specialist.
A tight oxygen cap drives Crabtree-like acetate overflow in glucose-replete dFBA on the E. coli core model.
A single well-mixed shared pool (no spatial structure) is sufficient to expose cross-feeding.

biological_summary:
Two E. coli populations sit in the same flask, drawing on one pool of glucose and acetate. They are not different organisms — both run the same core metabolic network — but they are tuned to different niches. One is a glucose specialist: it takes up glucose fast, but its oxygen supply is capped, so like real E. coli growing quickly it cannot fully burn the sugar and spills the excess carbon out as acetate. The other is an acetate specialist: it is poor at glucose but avid for acetate.

Run forward, the community sorts itself into two acts. In the first, the glucose specialist blooms, multiplying about 116-fold while it strips the glucose to nothing by t=8.3. As it grows it pumps acetate into the shared pool, which climbs to a transient peak of 17 mM. In the second act the glucose is gone, but the flask is now full of acetate — exactly the feedstock the second species wants. The acetate specialist, which had barely moved during the glucose phase, now grows ~55-fold, and 93% of that growth happens after the acetate peak.

That temporal offset is the whole point. If the two populations were simply competing for one resource, the better competitor would exclude the other. Instead, the byproduct of the first species' metabolism becomes the niche of the second — cross-feeding. The model reproduces this from nothing more than two Monod uptake tunings, an oxygen cap, and a shared FBA pool, which is why it is a compact but complete demonstration of what the CRM-FBA composite can do.

literature_anchors.model_observable: substrates.acetate rises while substrates.glucose is consumed
literature_anchors.status_in_workspace: Verified — acetate pool peaks at 17 mM during the glucose phase

literature_anchors.expectation: Acetate secreted by one population can be re-consumed by another (cross-feeding).
literature_anchors.status_in_workspace: Verified — 93% of acetate-specialist growth is post-peak

findings.statement: The glucose specialist blooms ~116x (0.008 -> 0.930 gDW) and drives the shared glucose pool to 0 by t=8.3.
Oxygen-capped glucose oxidation overflows acetate into the shared pool, which peaks at 17.4 mM at t=8.25 — coincident with glucose exhaustion.

evidence.observed: acetate pool peak 17.4 mM at t=8.25; glucose exhausted t=8.3

findings.statement: The acetate specialist grows ~55x, with 93% of its biomass gain occurring after the acetate peak — niche differentiation by cross-feeding, not competitive exclusion.

evidence.observed: acetate-specialist biomass x55; 7% pre-peak vs 93% post-peak growth

findings.next_action: Add a negative control that removes the acetate specialist's acetate uptake and confirm its growth collapses.

regression_compatibility.basis: The crm_fba_community composite builds and runs 360 steps to completion with no solver errors; run persisted to runs.db.

biological_validation.basis: All three behaviours pass: glucose->0, acetate overflow peak (17.4 mM), and 93% post-peak acetate-specialist growth — the predicted cross-feeding signature.

explanatory_gain.basis: The community sorts into two temporally offset growth phases from only two Monod tunings + an O2 cap + a shared pool, distinguishing cross-feeding from competition (F-03).

robustness.note: Dynamic FBA here is deterministic (fixed LP + Monod kinetics), so a single run is reproducible; a robustness sweep over the initial biomass split and O2 cap is the natural next step.

controls.name: acetate-uptake-knockout
controls.hypothesis: If the acetate specialist cannot take up acetate, its post-peak growth should collapse, isolating cross-feeding as the cause.
controls.expected: acetate-specialist biomass stays near its initial value after glucose is exhausted

alternative_hypotheses.claim: The acetate specialist grows by competing for glucose, not by consuming acetate.
alternative_hypotheses.discriminated_by: acetate-uptake-knockout control (pending) + the 93% post-peak growth timing

falsifiability: The cross-feeding claim is overturned if the acetate specialist's growth is unchanged when its acetate uptake is knocked out, or if the bulk of its growth occurs during the glucose phase (before the acetate peak).
limitations: Single well-mixed pool with no spatial structure or diffusion limitation.
Two hand-tuned Monod specialists on one shared GSM — not fitted to a specific co-culture dataset.
The negative control (acetate-uptake knockout) is declared but not yet run.
Deterministic single run; no multi-seed or parameter-sweep robustness yet.

resolved_uncertainties: The CRM-FBA composite can host a multi-species community on a shared pool and reproduce cross-feeding.
remaining_uncertainties: Whether cross-feeding survives an initial-biomass and O2-cap sweep.
Whether removing acetate uptake actually collapses the second growth phase (control pending).
